Day 6 In Class Assignment: A Scurry of Squirrels in Central Park#

✅ Put your name here.#

✅ Put your group member names here.

Learning Goals#

  • Write and use functions in Python with varying types of input parameters, default parameters, and types of return values

  • Explore the purpose and utility of functions in writing Python code

  • Write and use more complex functions using Boolean logic, loops, and if/else statements

Introduction#

Why are we doing this?#

When developing code, you will often be writing code that is meant to fit into a larger project, code that someone else (or future you) may use elsewhere, or code that needs to be used for massive amounts of data. In this assignment, you will practice writing code that others will need to use as well as code that needs to be combined into a larger project. You will also apply your function to a large data set to explore how functions can help when you want to get information form a very large data set.

Getting Started#

In this assignment, you will work in smaller groups and with your group to write and combine functions to explore data from the 2018 Central Park Squirrel Census. Your end goal is to use your functions from Part 1 to write new functions and extract information from data in Part 2.

During the first part of the assignment, you should not communciate with those in your group who are working on the other function (i.e. the one you’re not working on) once you beging coding. Rather, you should write a function with your small group that your remaing large group members would be able to use without any in depth instruction.

Make sure you write comments, use descriptive variable names, and make sure that your function will work in any notebook!

Part 1: Writing Functions in Small Groups#

First, divide your table into two groups. Each group will be responsible for one of the two functions you need to develop for Part 1. In the second part of the assignment, you will come together as a whole group, share your functions, and practice calling a function from another function. In the third part of today’s assignment, you will combine the functions you all develop in Part 1 into the function squirrel_data_summary found in Part 3. Pay attention to the variables types for inputs and returns.

The exact requirements for each function are listed in Part 1.2, but the basic idea for each function is the following:

  1. A function that takes in a list for the shift the squirrel was observed during (‘AM’ or ‘PM’) and returns the total number of squirrels observed in each shift. That means your function should return two values.

  2. A function that takes in a list of primary fur colors and returns a list of all the unique colors of the squirrels.

In the cell below, there are two lists to use for testing. The squirrel_shift list is for testing function 1, and the squirrel_primary_fur_color list is for testing function 2. Below is a description of what the data in each list means. Read the descriptions before you start coding!

About the Data#

You can assume that the indices for each individual list correspond to the same squirrel. That is, the 0-th element of squirrel_shift corresponds to the same squirrel as the 0-th element of any other provided squirrel lists.

  • squirrel_shift contains a string ‘AM’ or ‘PM’ for each element that indicates whether the squirrel was observed in the AM of the day or PM of the day.

  • squirrel_primary_fur_color contains a string for each element that indicates the primary fur color of the squirrel.

# sample data from 2018 Central Park Squirrel census 
squirrel_primary_fur_color = ["Gray", "White", "Black", "Gray"]
squirrel_shift = ["AM","AM","PM","AM"]

1.2 Helpful Hints and Guidance for each Function#

Now break into two groups and use the information below to guide your plan for the function you and the rest of your small group are going to write!

Function 1: Determining How Many Squirrels Were Observed in a Shift#

Your function should do the following:

  • Take in a list containing the shifts the squirrels were observed in (use the test data as an example)

  • Use a loop and if/else statements to check if the shift is ‘AM’ or ‘PM’

  • Count up how many squirrels were observed in the AM shift and how many were observed in the PM shift

  • Return the the totals for the two shifts

Function 2: Getting a List of Unique Fur Colors#

Your function should do the following:

  • Take in a list of fur color data (use the test data as an example)

  • Create a list that can be used to keep track of the unique colors of squirrels

  • Loop over the list of all squirrel colors using a for or while loop

  • Use if/else statements to determine if the color should be added to you list of unique colors or not

  • Add unique colors to your list as you find them

  • Return the list of unique colors

If you aren’t sure how to look for a specific value or values in a list, you can read about the uses of in when writing Python code here. You can also check if something not in a list using not in.

Part 5: Reflections#

Sometimes, throughout the semester, we will ask you to refect on your experiences as a tool to help you self-assess your understanding of course material and how you are feeling about your own work and your group’s work. Please answer the guiding questions below as completely as you can, even if you did not complete Part 2.

  1. What challenges did your group encounter while developing the functions for today’s class (in your pairs and full group)?

  2. Today’s assignment required a mix of small and larger group work. How well do you feel that you contributed to your group in that setting? How did your group work together in general?

  3. If your group had challenges working together, what changes should your group make going forward to work together more effectively? What changes can you make to your own contributions?

  4. Functions are a challenging topic in learning to write code to solve problems. If you were tutoring a student in CMSE 201, how would you explain functions to them?

  5. We still have quite a bit of the semester left, how do you see yourself using functions in your code throughout the semester?
